description: Somos Mecha-nology, un equipo de estudiantes de Mecatrónica Industrial especializados en el desarrollo de hardware, automatización y diseño 3D. Nuestro objetivo principal es construir el puente entre el mundo digital y el físico, usando microcontroladores y sensores.
summary: Twin Terra is an interactive digital mapping platform integrated with a self-leveling robotic lander module, designed to identify and validate Earth analog sites for missions toward future permanent bases on the Moon and Mars.   We address the high risk of the Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) phase by selecting locations of high geomorphological and atmospheric fidelity—Pampas de La Joya in Peru, the Salvador Dalí Desert in Bolivia, and Tolbachik in Russia—validated with NASA satellite data. Our web platform delineates safe zones and sends real-time slopes to a physical prototype of a parallel platform with an inertial sensor, capable of replicating extraterrestrial inclinations and automatically stabilizing itself to a horizontal level.   This system is key because it overcomes the limitations of conventional laboratories, reducing the risk of tip-over and ensuring the reliable deployment of future space infrastructure.
details:
1. What exactly does the project do?

Mecha-nology is a comprehensive hardware and software system that combines an interactive digital mapping platform with a Self-Leveling Robotic Lander Module to validate Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) protocols toward future permanent bases on the Moon and Mars. Specifically:

  • Identifies and characterizes Earth analog sites: Evaluates environments of high geomorphological and atmospheric fidelity on Earth—Pampas de La Joya (Peru) and the Salvador Dalí Desert / Puna (Bolivia) for Mars, alongside the Tolbachik Volcanic Field (Russia) for the Moon—integrating real NASA satellite data.
  • Physically simulates extraterrestrial slopes: Through a two-base parallel platform driven by three MG90SR servomotors and connected to the web via Web Serial, the robot reproduces in real time the Pitch and Roll tilt angles extracted directly from topographic maps of the Moon, Mars, or the analog sites.
  • Executes closed-loop self-leveling: Incorporates an inertial measurement unit (MPU6050) and an ESP32 microcontroller that compensate for terrain disturbances in milliseconds, keeping the cabin and communication systems leveled at 0.0° and triggering visual alerts if the critical 15° tip-over threshold is exceeded.
  1. How does it work? The system operates by integrating digital simulation and physical validation across four stages:
  • Geomorphological and Climatic Characterization (NASA Data): Topographic parameters (slopes, obstacles, albedo) and meteorological time series are extracted via NASA POWER (MERRA-2) and the PDS to delineate safe perimeters at the Earth analog sites and candidate zones on the Moon and Mars.
  • Cartographic Web Interface and Web Serial Transmission: From the interactive Mecha-nology web platform, the user selects real coordinates on the Moon, Mars, or the analog deserts. The web interface sends the actual terrain angles (Pitch, Roll) via the serial port at 115200 baud to the ESP32 microcontroller.
  • Parallel Kinematics and Actuation, Mode 2 - Terrain Simulation: With the lower base resting on the table, the ESP32 drives three MG90SR servomotors using guided crank-connecting rod mechanisms, tilting the upper base to precisely replicate the slope of the selected map and triggering an alert if the inclination exceeds 15°.
  • Real-Time Self-Leveling Control, Mode 1 - Stabilization: Upon activating autonomous mode via a physical button or from the web interface, the MPU6050 sensor connected via a 3.3V I2C bus continuously measures the actual angular deviation of the platform. The closed-loop control differentially adjusts the height of each leg in less than 20ms until the module is stabilized at 0.0°, preventing tip-overs like those seen in recent missions.
  1. What tools, languages, hardware, and software do we use?
  • Hardware and Electronics: ESP32 microcontroller, MPU6050 accelerometer/gyroscope inertial sensor, 3 high-torque MG90S servomotors, dedicated voltage regulator (5.8V–6.0V), and alert LED.
  • Manufacturing and Mechanical Design: Dual-base structure in 3mm PLA, vertical connecting rods, U-shaped sliding guides, and arm extenders 3D-printed in PLA with calibrated tolerances.
  • Firmware and Control: C++ / PlatformIO programming with a PID/differential closed-loop control system and high-speed serial communication (115200 baud).
  • Web Software and NASA Data: Interactive web platform with Web Serial API for live hardware-software linking, NASA POWER (MERRA-2), NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), and NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS).

4.  What benefits does it offer? It reduces the risk of tip-over during the critical Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) phase by uniting NASA satellite cartography with a physical platform capable of reproducing and compensating for real slopes in a single, low-cost testbed. It allows teams to validate sensors, leveling algorithms, and analog site selection criteria before deploying robotic or crewed missions. What is the expected impact?: In the short term, to offer an open educational and engineering tool where any team can test stabilization algorithms on real topographies of the Moon, Mars, and South America. In the long term, to contribute to the design of safer adaptive landing gear for establishing permanent bases at the lunar South Pole and on Mars.
